candidateRows: Scientists commonly accept an unsupported simplified narrative of chemical evolution despite lacking an evidential basis for it.
This establishes Tour’s central distinction between genuine scientific knowledge and a widely repeated origin-of-life narrative that he considers unsupported.
Swamidass’s suggestion that knowledgeable scientists already agree that the origin of the first life is unknown.
After Swamidass asks whether informed scientists already admit ignorance, Tour argues that most instead inherit a simple chemical-origin account from a small research community.
A natural origin of life cannot responsibly be called possible without chemically accounting for the production and assembly of all required molecular classes.
The move states the core pro-side standard: bare logical possibility is inadequate when the necessary chemistry and assembly pathways do not work or remain unspecified.
The moderator’s characterization of Tour’s objection as excessive confidence in a narrative that might merely be possible.
Tour intensifies his objection from public overconfidence to chemical feasibility, emphasizing that several molecular classes must be produced and assembled before possibility has substance.
An extremely small nonzero probability multiplied across an unimaginably large universe leaves the natural origin probability scientifically indeterminate.
This supplies the con side’s principal reason for evidential agnosticism: neither the tiny event probability nor the enormous number of opportunities is quantifiable.
Tour’s claim that the relevant chemistry is so improbable that natural origin scenarios lack substantive plausibility.
Swamidass obtains agreement that the probability is nonzero and that the universe is vastly larger than observed, then argues their product cannot presently be evaluated.
Appealing to a nonzero probability and a vast universe is scientifically empty unless a scenario specifies the molecules, their formation, their assembly, and cell formation.
The rebuttal directly challenges the con side’s probabilistic agnosticism by insisting that possibility claims require a chemically specified causal pathway.
Swamidass’s argument that a tiny nonzero probability across an unimaginably large universe produces an undefined overall probability.
Tour compares the probabilistic appeal to arbitrary unobserved possibilities and redirects the discussion toward concrete molecular production, assembly, and cellular organization.
Scientists should openly acknowledge that the origin of life is unexplained rather than presenting speculative accounts as established knowledge.
This connects the technical dispute to Tour’s broader central charge that institutional overstatement propagates false confidence across the academy and public.
Swamidass’s concession that he too does not know how life formed and his attempt to retain probabilistic agnosticism.
Following Swamidass’s admission of ignorance, Tour argues that the crucial failure is scientists’ reluctance to state that ignorance publicly while continuing to promote confident narratives.
Life as known requires four chemically difficult molecular classes whose correct production and integration into even a cell remain unexplained.
This is the pro side’s most developed chemical case, moving from precursor synthesis through stereochemistry, sequencing, membranes, interactions, and cellular organization.

Asked to contextualize why science is not close, Tour describes nucleic acids, lipids, amino acids, and carbohydrates, then argues that assembling them into a functional cell exceeds present capabilities.
Origin-of-life research has yielded limited clues even though those clues remain nowhere near a complete explanation.
The distinction between having no complete account and possessing some limited clues is central to the con side’s qualified agnosticism and directly frames the motion.
Tour’s repeated characterization of scientists as wholly clueless about how life first formed.
After Tour presses him to accept total ignorance, Swamidass distinguishes incomplete progress from no progress, describing a small advance that remains far from the goal.
Scientific advances reveal ever greater cellular complexity, so the explanatory target for origin-of-life research is receding rather than drawing closer.
This directly answers the motion’s temporal notion of meaningful progress by arguing that discovery has enlarged the unexplained target faster than proposed solutions advance.
Swamidass’s claim that researchers have ventured slightly toward an explanation despite remaining far from completing it.
Tour reverses Swamidass’s canyon analogy, arguing that early optimism rested on ignorance of cellular complexity and that newer findings continually expand what must be explained.
Long timescales hinder rather than rescue prebiotic synthesis because organic products decompose unless rapidly purified, stabilized, and advanced to subsequent reactions.
The move rebuts a major generic resource invoked for natural origin scenarios by explaining why additional time can destroy intermediates instead of accumulating progress.
The common response to origin-of-life difficulties that immense geological time makes otherwise unlikely chemical developments plausible.

Tour explains that synthesized organic molecules are normally isolated and cooled because exposure promotes decomposition and side reactions, making delayed multistep accumulation chemically problematic.
The scientifically warranted position is humble agnosticism because neither natural chemical emergence nor divine intervention has been demonstrated or excluded.
This is the con side’s clearest affirmative position on the motion, separating compatibility with faith from the limited evidential reach of current science.
Tour’s demand that Swamidass clearly state his position and his repeated insistence that scientific ignorance should be confessed.
Swamidass says either a natural pathway or direct divine action would fit his faith, while science lacks an accurate demonstrated account and should communicate its ideas with humility.
A nonzero overall probability does not overcome the many individually unfavorable chemical synthesis and assembly steps required for life.
This challenges the probabilistic basis for agnosticism by insisting that every required chemical step must be evaluated rather than collapsed into one abstract chance.
Swamidass's claim that an unquantified tiny probability multiplied by vast opportunities warrants scientific agnosticism.
After Swamidass describes life's origin as a possible statistical or thermodynamic miracle, Tour argues that synthesis and assembly require repeated unfavorable steps and concrete chemistry.
Independent extraterrestrial life would severely undermine the agnostic probability argument by showing that life arose more than once.
The proposed falsifier clarifies what empirical observation would materially shift the probability assessment away from evidential agnosticism.
Swamidass identifies independently originated exoplanetary life, sufficiently isolated from terrestrial seeding, as evidence that would show repeated origins within a defined space.
Finding life elsewhere would not explain how first life formed, and even two origins would leave the underlying chemical problem unresolved.
This directly contests the proposed evidential force of multiple origins by separating recurrence from a mechanistic account of origin-of-life chemistry.
Swamidass's position that independently arisen exoplanetary life would severely undermine his probability-based agnosticism.
Tour says the size of the universe and possible extraterrestrial creation do not reduce the difficulty of explaining first life, while allowing that a natural explanation may exist.
A universe teeming with independently arisen life would imply that life is naturally easy to make, but present observations show the opposite pattern.
The move connects observable prevalence of life to the ease of abiogenesis while acknowledging that transfer between worlds must first be excluded.
Tour's claim that discovering additional origins would not make the chemical problem of first life any easier.
Swamidass argues that widespread independent life would predict an accessible natural mechanism, whereas the apparently lifeless universe currently supplies no such signal.
Origin-of-life research may indicate a direction without nearing a solution, while an extraordinarily rare one-time origin could remain beyond scientific interrogation.
This articulates the con side's core middle position: limited directional clues can coexist with deep uncertainty and possible limits on what science can recover.
The audience analogy suggesting that origin-of-life science may show real progress despite an unknown distance from a final answer.
Swamidass grants only slight progress, then argues that a unique statistical event in an immense universe might be non-process-driven, unrepeatable, and scientifically inaccessible.
Origin-of-life targets are moving farther away, and repeated multistep laboratory syntheses are not advancing toward a plausible prebiotic pathway.
This supplies Tour's central empirical case that apparent research activity is not meaningful approach toward explaining life's origin and requires radically new methods.
The suggestion that origin-of-life research resembles gravitation research by making real progress despite remaining far from completion.
Tour contrasts origin-of-life work with progress on gravitation, says new findings make the target more remote, and criticizes staged laboratory syntheses as unproductive.
Long periods of confusion can precede rapid scientific progress after a conceptual breakthrough, so origin-of-life research could undergo a similar shift.
The analogy rebuts an inference from current stagnation to continued remoteness by emphasizing the historically discontinuous character of scientific progress.
Tour's argument that origin-of-life targets keep receding and current laboratory approaches are not producing meaningful progress.
Swamidass partly concedes Tour's diagnosis but notes that gravity advanced through insight and paradigm shifts, leaving open an analogous breakthrough for life's origin.
The probability of natural abiogenesis is greater than zero because chemical reactions have finite nonzero probabilities and chemistry is sufficient in principle.
This establishes a key premise of the agnostic probability argument even while allowing that the actual probability could be extraordinarily small.
The audience challenge asking how natural life's probability can be known to exceed zero without an exact definition of life.
Swamidass grounds a strictly nonzero probability in thermodynamics and chemical reactions, while emphasizing that the resulting chance might contain an enormous number of zeros.
Abiogenesis requires many separately improbable components and assembly steps, not merely one occurrence of a fully formed cell.
The distinction directly attacks treating abiogenesis as one probabilistic event and returns the assessment to the cumulative burdens of actual chemistry.
Swamidass's argument that thermodynamics makes natural abiogenesis nonzero and that the originating event need occur only once.
Tour agrees the value never reaches literal zero but argues that a cell does not appear in one step; its parts must first form and then assemble.
A recently dead cell does not spontaneously revive despite retaining nearly all its organization, showing that living systems remain mechanistically mysterious.
The example supports the broader claim that arranging molecular components is not yet an adequate explanation of the transition from nonlife to life.
Swamidass's claim that chemical reactions alone are sufficient in principle for life to arise with nonzero probability.
After stressing multistep assembly, Tour argues that even an intact cell that has just died does not restart, illustrating unresolved features of living organization.
